IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1421 OF 2024
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 8790 of 2024)

Manish Sisodia                                              ...Appellant
VERSUS
Central Bureau of Investigation & Directorate of Enforcement ...Respondents

CORAM:
HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE B.R. GAVAI
HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K.V. VISWANATHAN

J U D G M E N T
B.R. GAVAI, J.

1. Leave granted. The appellant calls in question the common judgment and order of the High Court of Delhi rejecting his second regular bail application under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in connection with RC No. 0032022A0053 registered by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

2. The allegations in the prosecution case emanate from the formulation and implementation of the Delhi Excise Policy 2021-22. The Central Bureau of Investigation registered offenses punishable under Section 120B read with Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 7, 7A and 12 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

3. Simultaneously, the Directorate of Enforcement registered ECIR/HIU-II/14/2022 alleging offenses under Sections 3 and 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 against the appellant and various co-accused individuals.

4. History of the Proceedings: The appellant was arrested by the CBI on 26th February 2023. Thereafter, he was arrested by the Directorate of Enforcement on 9th March 2023. The appellant has remained in continuous judicial custody since then.

5. The first round of bail applications culminated in the judgment of this Court dated 30th October 2023 in Criminal Appeal No. 3378 of 2023. While refusing bail at that juncture, this Court specifically granted liberty to the appellant to renew his prayer for bail if the trial proceeded at a snail's pace.

6. The Special Judge (CBI) dismissed the renewed bail application on 30th April 2024. The High Court affirmed the dismissal by the impugned order dated 21st May 2024, holding that the appellant wielded substantial political influence and could potentially tamper with prosecution witnesses or evidence.

7. Aggrieved by the refusal to grant regular bail, the appellant has approached this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.

8. Submissions on behalf of the Appellant: Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the appellant, submitted that the appellant has completed more than 17 months of incarceration without the commencement of trial.

9. Learned Senior Counsel urged that in both the CBI and ED proceedings, the investigation is exceedingly vast, with hundreds of witnesses and thousands of pages of documentary evidence yet to be scrutinized.

10. It was further submitted that out of 493 witnesses cited by the prosecution across multiple supplementary chargesheets, not a single witness has been examined till date. Charges have not yet been framed by the learned Special Judge.

11. Relying on the landmark judgment of this Court in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) 10 SCC 51, it was urged that prolonged pre-trial incarceration without reasonable prospect of trial conclusion amounts to punishment without conviction.

12. Learned Senior Counsel further highlighted that all electronic devices, mobile handsets, and digital records have already been seized by the investigating agencies. There is neither allegation nor apprehension that the appellant has attempted to tamper with digital forensic evidence during the investigation.

13. It was highlighted that co-accused persons who were attributed identical or greater roles have already been released on bail or interim bail by this Court and the High Court. The appellant is therefore entitled to parity in treatment under Article 14 and Article 21 of the Constitution.

14. The learned Senior Counsel adverted to the statutory compliance under Section 207 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, pointing out that supply of un-relied documents to the defense took months and the delay cannot be attributed to the appellant.

15. Submissions concluded with the emphasis that the right to speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21, and the statutory rigors of Section 45 of the PMLA cannot override the constitutional protection against indefinite detention.

16. Submissions on behalf of the Respondents: Mr. S.V. Raju, learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the CBI and ED, strenuously opposed the grant of bail. He submitted that the economic offences constitute a class apart and must be visited with a different approach in bail jurisprudence.

17. The learned ASG submitted that the appellant was the key architect of the excise policy and orchestrated a 12% profit margin for wholesalers to extract kickbacks of Rs. 100 crores for funding political activities.

18. It was contended that the twin conditions under Section 45(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 are mandatory and cannot be relaxed in serious financial crimes.

19. The respondent agencies argued that the delay in the trial was partly caused by the accused persons who filed repeated applications under Section 207 CrPC seeking inspection of voluminous un-relied documents.

20. The learned ASG placed reliance on Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022) SCC OnLine SC 929, asserting that the twin conditions are constitutional and the court must be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the accused is not guilty before ordering release.

21. It was further submitted that the appellant held the high public office of Deputy Chief Minister of Delhi and continues to exercise political authority, which creates an imminent risk of influencing vulnerable witnesses.

22. In rejoinder, learned counsel for the appellant reiterated that no trial involving 493 witnesses and 69,000 pages of documents could possibly conclude within any reasonable timeframe of 2 to 3 years.

23. Consideration and Judicial Analysis: We have heard learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant and the learned Additional Solicitor General for the respondents at great length and perused the extensive material on record.

24. The primary question that arises for our consideration is whether the appellant is entitled to be released on regular bail on the ground of delay in trial and prolonged incarceration in light of constitutional guarantees.

25. As early as in Babu Singh v. State of U.P. (1978) 1 SCC 579, Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer observed that our criminal justice system must not permit prolonged detention prior to conviction to become punitive in nature.

26. In Sanjay Chandra v. CBI (2012) 1 SCC 40, this Court reiterated that the object of bail is neither punitive nor preventive. Deprivation of liberty must be considered a punishment unless required by the exigencies of securing presence at trial.

27. While dealing with statutory restrictions such as Section 45 of PMLA or Section 43D(5) of UAPA, this Court in Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb (2021) 3 SCC 713 held that statutory restrictions do not oust the jurisdiction of constitutional courts to enforce Article 21.

28. We find that in the present case, the chargesheet runs into several volumes. There are 493 witnesses and thousands of pages of documents. The trial has not yet commenced and even the stage of framing charges under Section 228 CrPC has not arrived.

29. Keeping an accused behind bars for an indefinite period without any prospect of an early completion of trial is an antithesis to the rule of law and personal liberty guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution.

30. The trial court and the High Court erred in holding that the appellant alone was responsible for the delay. An accused cannot be penalized for exercising legitimate procedural rights under Section 207 CrPC to obtain copies of documents.
31. The assurance given by the prosecution in October 2023 that the trial would be concluded within six to eight months has completely failed to materialize.

32. The apprehension of the respondents that the appellant may tamper with evidence can be effectively mitigated by imposing stringent conditions, including surrendering his passport and refraining from entering the excise department.
33. In our considered opinion, where there is no realistic prospect of the trial concluding within a reasonable time, prolonged custody cannot be justified under the guise of economic gravity.
45. The appellant has been in custody for over 17 months. Prolonged incarceration without trial violates Article 21 of the Constitution. Bail is the rule and jail is an exception.

46. In view of the above, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court is set aside. The appellant Manish Sisodia is directed to be released on bail subject to furnishing personal bond in the sum of Rs. 10,00,000/- with two sureties of like amount.

key_dates.event: Supreme Court judgment granting regular bail

record.summary: The Supreme Court granted regular bail to appellant Manish Sisodia after 17 months of pre-trial custody in the Delhi Excise Policy case. The Bench reiterated that bail is the rule and jail is the exception, ruling that indefinite detention without trial infringes personal liberty under Article 21. The appellant was ordered to be released on a personal bond of Rs. 10,00,000.
record.summary_hi: सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने दिल्ली आबकारी नीति मामले में 17 महीने की हिरासत के बाद मनीष सिसोदिया को नियमित जमानत दे दी है। अदालत ने दोहराया कि जमानत नियम है और जेल अपवाद है, तथा बिना मुकदमे के लंबी हिरासत अनुच्छेद 21 के तहत स्वतंत्रता का उल्लंघन है।

brief.facts: Appellant was arrested in February-March 2023 by CBI and ED in connection with Delhi Excise Policy 2021-22 offenses under IPC, PC Act, and PMLA. He spent over 17 months in continuous pre-trial detention with 493 prosecution witnesses and over 69,000 pages of material.
issues: Whether prolonged incarceration without trial commencement violates the fundamental right to speedy trial under Article 21?
Whether statutory twin conditions under Section 45 of PMLA override constitutional protections against indefinite detention without trial?
brief.arguments: Appellant contended that 17 months custody without a single examined witness violates personal liberty and speedy trial rights under Article 21. Respondents submitted that serious economic offences involve mandatory twin bail conditions under PMLA Section 45 and risk of witness tampering.
brief.reasoning: The Court held that bail is the rule and jail is the exception. Prolonged incarceration without reasonable prospect of timely trial infringes Article 21. Section 45 PMLA cannot be read to permit indefinite detention without trial.
brief.decision: Appeal allowed. Impugned High Court order set aside. Regular bail granted subject to personal bond of Rs. 10,00,000 and two sureties.
